title: How Fever Dreams Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain fevers and dreams to set up a discussion of fever dreams. They open with tour announcements and candy banter, then cover normal body temperature (the 98.6 F figure traced to Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich's 1868 work), hypothalamus regulation tied to the daily temperature cycle, pyrogens and how infection triggers fever, fever thresholds for adults and children, and sympathetic nervous system effects. They then cover dream science: the activation-synthesis hypothesis, threat simulation theory, the Italian EEG study supporting affect regulation theory, and nightmares. The fever dream section offers an anecdotal explanation: a fevered brain under stress, amygdala overactivity, and waking during REM when body temperature is no longer regulated. The episode closes with a listener fan mail letter about the puberty episodes and tour dates.

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Tour dates and ticket info (sysklive.com), followed by casual banter about candy, Pop Rocks, and unicorn pizza. Not really a sponsor read; this is opening chatter.

segments.title: Introduction to fevers and body temperature
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic of fever dreams, noting that little research exists on them. They discuss the normal body temperature of 98.6 F and its origin in Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich's 1868 study, and note that normal temperature varies over the day.

segments.title: Circadian temperature and the hypothalamus
segments.summary: Body temperature is regulated by the hypothalamus. It peaks in the late afternoon, associated with alertness, falls toward drowsiness, and is lowest just before waking, which is associated with REM sleep.

segments.title: How infection causes fever (pyrogens)
segments.summary: Infection triggers the immune system to release pyrogens, which travel to the hypothalamus, dampen heat-sensing neurons and excite cold-sensing neurons, so the body raises its temperature. The fever helps fight pathogens but makes the body feel bad and strains organs; sympathetic nervous system activation is mentioned.
topics: feed a cold starve a fever

segments.title: Fever thresholds for adults and children
segments.summary: Fever is defined as oral temperature above 100.4 F (written as one point four) or rectal or ear above 101 F in adults. Children's fevers can spike faster because their immune systems are less experienced. Hosts advise consulting a doctor and note they are not medical experts.

segments.title: Dream science: theories and the Italian EEG study
segments.summary: Older activation-synthesis hypothesis (random neural firing) is contrasted with psychoanalytic views and threat simulation theory. An Italian study using EEG and waking subjects found frontal theta waves linked to dream recall, supporting affect regulation theory, under which dreams process emotions into memories.

segments.title: Nightmares and the theory of fever dreams
segments.summary: Nightmares are explained as emotions overwhelming the memory-processing process. Fever dreams are described as nightmares on steroids. Anecdotally they seem more common in childhood, and the hosts propose that a fevered brain under heat stress, amygdala overactivity, and waking during REM when temperature regulation is off could make them more vivid.

segments.title: Anxiety dreams and recreational drugs
segments.summary: Chuck describes his own anxiety dreams, which he attributes to watching Fargo. The hosts briefly note that meth and ecstasy can raise brain temperature, which may contribute to brain cell death.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A fan letter praises the hosts' puberty episodes. The hosts briefly discuss DC live show logistics, then close with social media and website information.
